notes.about: Micah names seven shepherds, then raises the count to eight. The numbers are not an exact count: they promise leaders enough to stand against the invader, and some read the eight as more than enough. Job 5:19 and Ecclesiastes 11:2 count the same way.

figure.name: Numerical saying
figure.words: seven shepherds, even eight leaders of men
figure.means: a full number of leaders, enough to meet the invader, and the eight goes past the seven

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): seven would be enough, and eight goes past it, as if there might be more than needed. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls seven and eight an idiom for a full and sufficient number. John Calvin says a great number is meant; E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes), that eight goes past the sacred whole of seven; Matthew Henry, enough men, an inexact number.
notes.limit: The writers agree the numbers are not an exact count. They differ on how many are meant, enough for the need or a great many, and they read the shepherds and leaders in different ways.

cites.quote: Seven is mentioned as the number of the works proceeding from God, so that seven shepherds, i.e., princes, would be quite sufficient; and this number is surpassed by the eight, to express the thought that there might be even more than were required.

cites.quote: "Seven" expresses perfection; "seven and eight" is an idiom for a full and sufficient number

cites.quote: By seven and eight, the Prophet no doubt meant a great number. ... But the Prophet says here that there would be many leaders to undertake the care of ruling and defending the people.
The "seven" is throughout the Old Testament a symbol of a sacred whole, probably of the union of God with the world, reconciled with it; eight, when united with it, is something beyond it.

cites.quote: Then shall we raise against him seven shepherds and eight principal men, that is, a competent number of persons, proper to oppose the enemy, and make head against him ... Seven and eight are a certain number for an uncertain.

notes.short: Sow, press, tread, and never enjoy it
notes.about: Three lines built the same way: you will sow but not reap, press olives but not anoint yourselves, tread grapes but not drink the wine. Each line names a labor and then the loss of its fruit.

lines.words: You will sow but not reap;
you will press olives but not anoint yourselves with oil;
you will tread grapes but not drink the wine.

notes.evidence: Lowth says stanzas of three lines are most often parallel by construction, and gives this verse among his examples of three-line stanzas that are constructively parallel.
